Chapter 16 · Putting It Together

Project: Notes API Server

Time to combine everything into one real application: a REST API for notes with a JSON file store, validation, structured logging, live change events, graceful shutdown, a command-line client and an automated test suite — with zero npm dependencies. Every file is shown in full, and the finished project is in playground/reference/.

You will build

  • A REST API: GET/POST /notes, GET/PATCH/DELETE /notes/:id, filtering by tag and text, and GET /health.
  • A NotesStore that emits events and saves to disk atomically, with writes queued so they never overlap.
  • Validation with clear 4xx errors, a body-size limit, and generic 500s for bugs.
  • GET /events: server-sent events streaming every change live.
  • Config from environment variables, JSON logs with request ids, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM.
  • A notes CLI that talks to the API with fetch, and tests with node:test.

The design

DecisionWhyChapter
A factory createApp({ store, logger }) that doesn't listentests start it on port 0 with a temporary store; no globals14
Store writes are chained on one promisetwo requests can't save at the same time and corrupt the file6, 9
Write to a temp file, then renamea crash never leaves half a JSON file9
Expected failures are HttpErrors; everything else is a logged 500clear errors for clients, no leaked internals11, 15
The store is an EventEmitterlive updates (SSE) without the store knowing about HTTP8
No dependenciesnothing to audit or update; everything here is built into Node4

Step 1: package.json

Create a folder notes-api (or use playground/) with this package.json. The bin field makes npx notes run the CLI, and the scripts cover running, developing and testing.

Step 2: configuration and logging

Every setting comes from the environment, with a default, and is validated once at startup: a typo like PORT=80800 stops the server immediately with a clear message instead of failing later in a confusing way. The result is frozen so nothing changes settings at run time.

This is the logger from Chapter 15, plus a silent level for tests and an out option so a test could capture the lines.

Step 3: errors and the store

  • load() treats a missing file as "no notes yet" (ENOENT) but rethrows anything else, such as corrupt JSON — you want to know about that.
  • #save() captures a snapshot of the data synchronously, then chains the write onto #saving. Each write waits for the previous one, so the file is always written in order.
  • Events are emitted only after the save succeeded, so listeners never announce a change that didn't happen.

🧠 Analogy: one shared printer. If ten people send a document to the same printer at once, the printer doesn't interleave their pages: it queues the jobs and prints them one after another. #saving is that print queue. Without it, two overlapping writeFile+rename sequences could finish in the wrong order and an older snapshot could overwrite a newer one.

Step 4: the router

match returns either a handler with its path parameters, or a status: 404 when no route has that path, 405 when the path exists with other methods. Keeping matching separate from responding makes it trivial to test.

Step 5: the HTTP application

  • validateNote collects all problems and returns only known fields, so a client can't sneak in an id or createdAt. With partial: true it validates PATCH bodies.
  • readJson checks the content type, enforces the size limit while streaming (it stops reading as soon as the limit is passed), and insists on a JSON object.
  • Every request gets a short request id and one log line when the response finishes, with method, URL, status and duration.
  • /events uses events.on for each event type with a signal that aborts when the client disconnects, so no listener is ever leaked (Chapter 8, Exercise 9).
  • The outer try/catch turns HttpErrors into JSON responses and everything else into a logged 500. If headers were already sent (a streaming response), it destroys the connection instead.

Step 6: the server entry point

startServer is exported so scripts and tests can start the real thing with a custom environment; the import.meta.main block runs only when you execute node src/server.js. On SIGINT/SIGTERM it marks itself unhealthy, stops accepting connections, closes idle ones, and force-closes the rest after 5 seconds.

Step 7: the CLI client

The CLI is a thin layer: parseArgs for options (-t may repeat), fetch with a timeout, the API's error messages shown in red on stderr, and exit code 1 on failure so scripts can react. Colours disappear automatically when output isn't a terminal.

Step 8: tests

Each test gets a fresh store in a temporary folder and a fresh server on a random port, so tests are independent. They cover the full CRUD cycle, filtering, every error status, persistence across store instances, and the live event stream.

Step 9: an end-to-end smoke test

Unit and HTTP tests check the parts. A smoke test checks the assembled system: it starts the real server with startServer, runs the real CLI as child processes (Chapter 13), and shuts down gracefully:

Recap

  • Structure: config → logger → store → app → server, each a small module with one job, wired together in server.js.
  • Factories with injected dependencies (createApp({ store, logger }), startServer(env)) make the whole app testable without mocks.
  • Correctness under concurrency: chained, atomic writes; events after successful saves; listeners removed on disconnect.
  • Robust HTTP: content-type and size checks, validation that lists every problem, HttpError → status, generic 500s, request logs.
  • Operable: env config, JSON logs, health endpoint, graceful shutdown, a CLI with proper exit codes, and tests from unit to end-to-end.

Exercises

Each exercise extends the project in playground/ (copy playground/reference first; no playground yet? Clone it from coder-hop/nodejs-book-playground). Run npm test after every change.

Exercise 1 🟢 easy extend

Add a GET /notes/count route that returns { "total": n, "done": d }. Where must it be registered relative to /notes/:id, and why?

Show solution

Register it before /notes/:id: the router returns the first matching route, and :id would also match count (and then fail with "id must be a positive integer").

Exercise 2 🟢 easy config

What happens when you start the server with PORT=abc? And with MAX_BODY_BYTES=50? Check with loadConfig directly.

Show solution

The server refuses to start with a clear message (failing fast at startup), instead of misbehaving later.

Exercise 3 🟢 easy CLI

Add an undone <id> command to the CLI that sets done back to false, and a --json flag for list that prints the raw JSON instead of the formatted lines.

Show solution

--json output is meant for other programs (notes list --json | jq …), so keep it free of colours and extra text.

Exercise 4 🟢 easy explain

Why does the store emit "created" only after await this.#save(), and what could go wrong if it emitted before saving?

Show solution

If saving fails (disk full, permissions), the request gets an error and the note doesn't exist on disk. Emitting first would already have told every /events client that the note was created — a change that then "disappears" on restart. Announcing only completed changes keeps listeners consistent with the persisted state.

Exercise 5 🟡 medium pagination

Add ?limit= (default 20, max 100) and ?offset= to GET /notes, returning { items, total, limit, offset }. Invalid values give a 400. Write the helper and test it on its own.

Show solution

In the route: send(res, 200, paginate(store.list({ … }), query)). Changing the response shape is a breaking change for clients (the CLI!), so real APIs version it or add pagination from day one.

Exercise 6 🟡 medium auth

Protect all write routes (POST, PATCH, DELETE) with an API key: requests must send Authorization: Bearer <key> matching process.env.API_KEY, compared in constant time, or get 401. Reads stay public. Sketch the check and test the comparison.

Show solution

Call requireApiKey(req, apiKey) at the top of the request handler (inside the try), add an apiKey option to createApp, and make the CLI send the header from NOTES_API_KEY. The logger already redacts authorization.

Exercise 7 🟡 medium test

Write a test proving the store's write queue works: start 20 create calls without awaiting them individually, then check that a fresh store loading the file sees all 20 notes with ids 1–20.

Show solution

Try removing the chaining in #save() (write directly each time) and run the test a few times: overlapping renames can leave an older snapshot on disk.

Exercise 8 🟡 medium rate limit

Plug the rateLimit middleware from Chapter 11 (Exercise 10) into server.js, configured by RATE_LIMIT (requests per minute, default 120). Which requests should count, and what should /health do?

Show solution

Wrap the app's request handler: const limited = rateLimit({ limit: config.rateLimit, windowMs: 60_000 }); and create the server with http.createServer(limited(handler)) — so createApp needs to expose its handler (or accept a wrap option). Exclude /health from the limit: the load balancer polls it constantly and must never be refused, or it will take the instance out of service. Count everything else per client IP, and remember the counters are per process (Chapter 13): with several replicas, use a shared store.

Exercise 9 🔴 hard SQLite

Replace the JSON file with SQLite using the built-in node:sqlite module: write a SqliteNotesStore with the same public methods and events (load, list, get, create, update, remove). Tags can be stored as a JSON string. Show it working.

Show solution

Because the app only depends on the store's methods and events, swapping the storage needs no change to app.js — just construct a different store in server.js. Parameterised statements (?) prevent SQL injection. (DatabaseSync is synchronous: fine for small, local data; heavy queries would block the event loop.)

Exercise 10 🔴 hard production

Write a deployment checklist for this service running in a container behind a load balancer: what to set, what to monitor, and three changes you'd make to the code before real users arrive.

Show solution
  • Run: Node LTS, NODE_ENV=production, npm ci --omit=dev, a non-root user, node --permission --allow-fs-read=/app --allow-fs-write=/app/data src/server.js, PORT/DATA_FILE/LOG_LEVEL from the platform, data on a persistent volume.
  • Platform: point liveness and readiness checks at /health; send SIGTERM on deploys with a grace period longer than 5 s; one replica only while storage is a single JSON file.
  • Monitor: request rate, error rate (5xx), latency percentiles from the request logs; event-loop delay; memory; disk space for the data file; alerts on restarts.
  • Code changes: (1) move storage to a real database (Exercise 9 or PostgreSQL) so you can run several replicas; (2) add authentication (Exercise 6) and rate limiting (Exercise 8); (3) add pagination (Exercise 5) and a cap on the number of open /events connections, plus a heartbeat comment every 30 s so proxies don't close idle streams.
